verses.translation: Yehudah{H3063}, a servant{H5650} of Yeshua{H3442} the Mashiach{H4899}, but one{H259} brother{H251} of Ya'aqov{H3290} the sent-one{H7971}. To the sanctified-ones{H6942} in YHWH{H3068} the Father{H1}, and the hidden-ones{H5641} in Yeshua{H3442} the Mashiach{H4899}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שָׁלִיחַ (shaliach — 'sent-one', from shalach H7971) — a native Hebrew word for emissary/delegate. Greek has no corresponding title here at all (simply Ἰούδας... δοῦλος... ἀδελφός). If this were a back-translation from Greek, there would be no reason to add a title the Greek lacks. The Hebrew author uses שליח exactly as it appears in Revelation 21:14 (שלוחים for 'apostles'), a consistent Hebrew authorship vocabulary.

Uses נִסְתָּרִים (nistarim — 'hidden ones', from satar H5641). Greek has τετηρημένοις ('kept/preserved'). A back-translator from Greek would use שְׁמוּרִים (shemurim — 'kept/guarded'), not nistarim. The Hebrew concept of being 'hidden' in the Mashiach carries the mystical overtone of Psalm 27:5 — 'in the day of evil he shall hide me (יַסְתִּרֵנִי) in his tabernacle.' The Greek 'kept' lacks this Psalm-rooted theology.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds הַשָּׁלִיחַ ('the sent-one') — absent from Greek entirely.
Hebrew: 'hidden' (נסתרים). Greek: 'kept/preserved' (τετηρημένοις). Different concept.
Greek adds κλητοῖς ('called ones') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Sent-one' for shaliach — the native Hebrew equivalent of 'apostle,' preserving the Hebraic meaning (one sent on a mission) without importing the Greek loanword.
'Hidden-ones' for nistarim — this is the nistar concept from the Torah (Deut 29:29 — 'the hidden things belong to YHWH'), applied to believers concealed within divine protection.

verses.translation: YHWH{H3068} will give{H5414} to you much{H7235} love{H160} and chesed{H2617} and peace{H7965} and compassion{H7356}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֶסֶד (chesed, H2617) — the untranslatable Hebrew covenant-loyalty word (Gen 24:12, Ex 15:13, Ps 136). Greek has ἔλεος ('mercy'). Chesed encompasses mercy, kindness, loyalty, and covenant faithfulness — no single Greek word captures it. A back-translator from Greek ἔλεος would use רַחֲמִים (rachamim — 'mercy'), not the theologically heavier chesed.

Hebrew has YHWH as active subject: 'YHWH will give to you.' Greek uses passive: πληθυνθείη ('may it be multiplied'). The Hebrew has a direct divine actor; the Greek has an impersonal passive. A back-translator from the Greek passive would write יִרְבּוּ לָכֶם ('may they be multiplied to you'), not 'YHWH will give.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: four blessings — love, chesed, peace, compassion. Greek: three — mercy, peace, love. Different number and different order.
Hebrew: 'YHWH will give' (active). Greek: 'may it be multiplied' (passive). Different grammatical voice and subject.
Hebrew has רַחֲמִים (compassion) — absent from Greek entirely.
translation_notes: 'Chesed' left untranslated to preserve the uniquely Hebrew covenant concept. No English word captures its full range.
textual_notes: The Hebrew greeting formula echoes Numbers 6:24-26 (the Aaronic blessing) in structure — YHWH as active giver of peace and chesed.

verses.translation: Beloved{H157} brothers{H251}, after{H310} I desired{H7521} to write{H3789} to you concerning our holiness{H6944}, I found{H4672} it necessary to prove{H3198} to you in the writings{H3791} that you should strengthen{H2388} yourselves in the faith{H530} that was given{H5414} to the holy-ones{H6918}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קְדוּשָּׁה (qedushah — 'holiness', H6944). Greek has σωτηρίας ('salvation'). A back-translator from Greek would write יְשׁוּעָה (yeshuah — 'salvation'), NOT qedushah ('holiness'). These are fundamentally different concepts — the Hebrew emphasizes sanctification, the Greek emphasizes rescue. The Hebrew author's concern is holiness, not soteriology.

Uses לְהוֹכִיחַ... בִּכְתָבִים ('to prove... in the writings', from yakach H3198). The verb yakach means to argue a case, prove, rebuke — a forensic/legal term (Gen 20:16, Job 13:15, Isa 1:18). Greek has παρακαλῶν ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι ('exhorting you to contend'). The Hebrew says 'prove from Scripture'; the Greek says 'contend for the faith.' A back-translator would never produce yakach ('forensically prove') from parakaleo ('exhort').

Uses תְּחַזְּקוּ (techazqu — 'strengthen', from chazaq H2388). Greek has ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι ('contend/fight'). Strengthening oneself in faith vs. fighting for faith — different metaphors. A back-translator from Greek would use הִלָּחֵם (nilcham — 'fight'), not chazaq ('strengthen').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'our holiness' (קדושתנו). Greek: 'our common salvation' (κοινῆς σωτηρίας). Different topic entirely.
Hebrew: 'prove to you in the writings' (forensic-scriptural argument). Greek: 'exhorting you to contend' (athletic/military metaphor).
Hebrew: 'strengthen yourselves in the faith.' Greek: 'contend for the faith once delivered.' Different verb and concept.
translation_notes: 'Prove' for yakach — the forensic/legal sense of establishing a case through evidence, specifically from 'the writings' (כתבים — Scriptures).
textual_notes: כְתָבִים (ketavim — 'writings') is the standard Hebrew term for Scriptures (cf. Daniel 10:21 — כְּתָב אֱמֶת 'writing of truth'). The Hebrew Jude appeals to scriptural proof; the Greek Jude appeals to contention.

verses.translation: For certain{H376} sons{H1121} of adam{H120} have come{H935} among them, from those already{H3528} written{H3789} for this punishment{H6066}, and they are wicked{H7563} and withhold the chesed{H2617} from YHWH{H3068} with presumption{H2087}, and do not believe{H539} in YHWH{H3068} and in his Mashiach{H4899}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּמֵזִיד (be-mezid — 'with presumption/deliberately', from zud H2087). This is the specific Torah legal term for high-handed, deliberate sin — as opposed to בִּשְׁגָגָה (be-shgagah — inadvertent sin). Numbers 15:30: 'the soul that does anything with a high hand (בְּיָד רָמָה)... presumptuously (mezid).' Deuteronomy 17:12, 18:22 use the same root for presumptuous defiance. Greek has ἀσέλγειαν ('lasciviousness/sensuality') — a completely different moral category. A back-translator from Greek ἀσέλγεια would write זִמָּה (zimmah — 'lewdness') or תַּאֲוָה (ta'avah — 'lust'), NEVER the Torah's legal term mezid. The Hebrew author categorizes their sin using Torah jurisprudence; the Greek translator substitutes a Greek moral concept.

Uses מְעַכְּבִים הַחֶסֶד ('withhold the chesed'). Greek has τὴν χάριν μετατιθέντες ('perverting/changing the grace'). Hebrew: they BLOCK God's chesed from reaching people. Greek: they PERVERT God's grace into something else. Different actions, different theology. A back-translator would write מְשַׁנִּים or מַחֲלִיפִים ('changing/exchanging'), not מְעַכְּבִים ('withholding').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sons of adam' (בני אדם). Greek: 'certain men' (τινες ἄνθρωποι). Hebrew uses the more Hebraic expression.
Hebrew: 'with presumption' (במזיד — Torah legal category). Greek: 'into lasciviousness' (εἰς ἀσέλγειαν — moral category). Completely different.
Hebrew: 'withhold the chesed.' Greek: 'pervert the grace.' Different verb and concept.
Hebrew: 'do not believe in YHWH and in his Mashiach.' Greek: 'deny the only Master God and our Lord Jesus Christ' (ἀρνούμενοι). Not-believing vs. denying.
translation_notes: 'Presumption' for mezid preserves the Torah legal category — deliberate, high-handed sin against known commandments (Numbers 15:30-31).
textual_notes: The mezid/shgagah distinction is foundational to Torah jurisprudence. Inadvertent sin (shgagah) could be atoned through sacrifice (Lev 4-5). Presumptuous sin (mezid) resulted in being 'cut off' from the people (Num 15:30-31). The Hebrew Jude accuses these infiltrators of the most severe category of sin.

verses.translation: But I want{H7521} to inform{H3045} you of this: that the one who brought-out{H3318} his people{H5971} from Mitsrayim{H4714} put-to-death{H4191} a second{H8145} time{H6471} those who did not believe{H539}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הוֹצִיא (hotsi — 'brought out', hiphil of yatsa H3318) — THE Exodus verb. This is the word used in the Torah's defining statement: 'I am YHWH your God who brought you out (הוֹצֵאתִיךָ) of the land of Egypt' (Ex 20:2, Deut 5:6). Greek has σώσας ('having saved'). A back-translator from Greek σώζω would use הוֹשִׁיעַ (hoshia — 'saved'), not the specific Exodus verb hotsi. The Hebrew author instinctively uses the Torah's Exodus vocabulary.

Uses הֵמִית (hemit — 'put to death', hiphil of mut H4191) — a causative form meaning to execute/kill. Greek has ἀπώλεσεν ('destroyed'). Hebrew hemit is judicial execution; Greek apollumi is general destruction. A back-translator from Greek would use הֶאֱבִיד (he'evid — 'destroyed'), not the judicial death verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'brought out' (Exodus verb). Greek: 'having saved' (σώσας). Different framing of the same event.
Hebrew: 'put to death' (judicial). Greek: 'destroyed' (general). Different severity.
Greek specifies 'the Lord' (ὁ κύριος) as subject; Hebrew says 'the one who...' without naming — letting the reader supply the identity from Exodus knowledge.
translation_notes: 'Brought out' for hotsi preserves the Exodus connection. This is the verb that defines Israel's identity.

verses.translation: And also the messengers{H4397} who sinned{H2398} and were driven-out{H2778} from above{H4605} — they are hidden{H5641} in the darkness{H2822} until the future{H6256} day{H3117} of judgment{H1779}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׁחָטְאוּ (she-chat'u — 'who sinned', from chata H2398) — a single, direct word. Greek has a complex phrase: τοὺς μὴ τηρήσαντας τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχήν ἀλλὰ ἀπολιπόντας τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον ('who did not keep their first estate but left their own habitation'). The Hebrew says simply 'they sinned'; the Greek explains HOW they sinned. A back-translator from Greek would reproduce the elaborate description, not condense it to a single verb.

Uses נֶחְדְּפוּ (nechedefu — 'were driven out') — passive voice. They were EXPELLED. Greek has ἀπολιπόντας ('having left/abandoned') — active voice. They LEFT voluntarily. This is a fundamental theological difference: in the Hebrew, the angels were driven out by divine judgment; in the Greek, the angels voluntarily abandoned their station. A back-translator from the active Greek verb would write עָזְבוּ ('they left'), not the passive 'they were driven out.'

Uses נִסְתָּרִים (nistarim — 'hidden') again, matching verse 1. Greek has τετήρηκεν ('he has kept'). This is the second instance of the Hebrew nistar concept where Greek has 'keep' — a consistent Hebrew vocabulary pattern across the epistle.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'who sinned' (one verb). Greek: 'who did not keep their first estate but left their own habitation' (elaborate description).
Hebrew: 'were driven out from above' (passive — expelled). Greek: 'having left their own habitation' (active — voluntary departure).
Hebrew: 'hidden in the darkness.' Greek: 'kept in everlasting chains under darkness' (δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις ὑπὸ ζόφον τετήρηκεν). Greek adds 'everlasting chains' — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'the future day of judgment.' Greek: 'the judgment of the great day.' Future vs. great.
translation_notes: 'Driven out' preserves the passive voice — divine action against rebel angels, not voluntary departure.
'Hidden' for nistarim — same word used in verse 1 for believers 'hidden in Yeshua.' The righteous are hidden protectively; the fallen angels are hidden punitively. Same verb, opposite contexts.

verses.translation: And also the places{H4725} Sedom{H5467} and Amorah{H6017} and the like come as an example{H4912}, and they suffer{H5375} forever{H5769} the fire{H784} of Gehinnom{H1516}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses גֵּיהִנֹּם (Gehinnom) — the Valley of Hinnom (gey ben-Hinnom, H1516), the specific Hebrew concept of the place of judgment derived from 2 Kings 23:10, 2 Chronicles 28:3, 33:6, Jeremiah 7:31-32, 19:2-6, 32:35. Greek has πυρὸς αἰωνίου ('eternal fire') — a generic concept. A back-translator from Greek 'eternal fire' would write אֵשׁ עוֹלָם ('eternal fire'), NOT Gehinnom. The Hebrew uses the specific geographic-theological concept rooted in Jeremiah's prophecies about the Valley of Hinnom. This parallels Revelation 21:8's אֵשׁ הַשְּׁאוֹל ('fire of Sheol') vs. Greek 'lake of fire' — the same pattern of Hebrew-specific afterlife geography.

Uses מָשָׁל (mashal, H4912) — the Hebrew word for proverb, parable, example, warning-tale (Num 21:27, Deut 28:37, 1 Kings 9:7, Ezek 17:2). Greek has δεῖγμα ('example/sample'). Mashal carries far more weight — it implies a prophetic teaching-story, not merely an illustration.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'fire of Gehinnom' (specific Hebrew afterlife concept). Greek: 'eternal fire' (πυρὸς αἰωνίου — generic).

Hebrew: 'the places Sedom and Amorah' (מקומות — 'places'). Greek: cities 'in like manner' with 'going after strange flesh' (ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας). Greek adds 'going after strange flesh' — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'come as a mashal' (prophetic teaching-example). Greek: 'are set forth as a sample/example' (δεῖγμα — simple illustration).
translation_notes: 'Gehinnom' transliterated to preserve the Valley of Hinnom connection. This is not 'hell' in the Greek/medieval sense but the specific prophetic locale from Jeremiah.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 7:31-32 — 'They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the son of Hinnom... it shall no more be called Topheth, nor the Valley of the son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.' The Hebrew concept of Gehinnom as a place of judgment originates here.

verses.translation: And like these are those who despise{H959} the authority{H8323} and curse{H7043} the kingdom{H4438}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: two actions (despise authority, curse the kingdom). Greek: three actions — defile flesh (σάρκα μιαίνουσιν), reject authority (κυριότητα ἀθετοῦσιν), blaspheme glories (δόξας βλασφημοῦσιν). Greek adds 'defiling the flesh' — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι ('dreamers') — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: שררות ('authority', from sarar H8323 — 'to rule'). Greek: κυριότητα ('lordship'). Hebrew: מלכות ('kingdom', H4438). Greek: δόξας ('glories' — plural). Different vocabulary.
translation_notes: The concise Hebrew (two charges) vs. elaborate Greek (three charges plus 'dreamers') suggests the Hebrew is original and the Greek expanded for emphasis.

verses.translation: But the messenger{H4397} Mikha'el{H4317}, when{H8160} he disputed{H2505} with the Satan{H7854} over the grave{H6913} of Mosheh{H4872}, even so did not curse{H7043} him, but said{H559} to him: The Lord{H113} will punish{H6064} you.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַקֶּבֶר (ha-qever — 'the grave/burial-place', H6913). Greek has τοῦ Μωϋσέως σώματος ('the body of Moses'). The dispute is over Moses' GRAVE in the Hebrew, over his BODY in the Greek. Deuteronomy 34:6 says 'he buried him... but no man knows his burial-place (קְבֻרָתוֹ) to this day.' The Hebrew connects directly to this Torah mystery about Moses' unknown grave. A back-translator from Greek σῶμα ('body') would use גּוּף (guf — 'body') or גְּוִיָּה (geviyah — 'corpse'), NEVER קבר ('grave'). The Hebrew preserves the Deuteronomy 34 tradition; the Greek shifts to a different tradition.

Uses יַעֲנוֹשׁ (ya'anosh — 'will punish', from anash H6064). Greek has ἐπιτιμήσαι ('rebuke'). Punishing and rebuking are fundamentally different — one is judicial action, the other is verbal correction. A back-translator from Greek 'rebuke' would use יִגְעַר (yig'ar — 'rebuke', from ga'ar H1605, cf. Zech 3:2), not the judicial 'punish.' The Hebrew frames this as divine court; the Greek frames it as verbal correction.

Uses הַמַּלְאָךְ מִיכָאֵל ('the messenger Mikha'el'). Greek has ὁ Μιχαὴλ ὁ ἀρχάγγελος ('Michael the archangel'). The Hebrew uses the native term mal'akh (H4397 — 'messenger'); the Greek uses the compound ἀρχάγγελος ('arch-angel'). A back-translator from Greek would write שַׂר הַמַּלְאָכִים ('prince of the messengers') or transliterate ארכאנגל, not simply mal'akh.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the grave of Mosheh.' Greek: 'the body of Moses.' Different object of dispute.
Hebrew: 'will punish' (judicial). Greek: 'rebuke' (verbal). Different severity.
Hebrew: 'the messenger Mikha'el.' Greek: 'Michael the archangel.' Different title.
Hebrew: 'even so did not curse him' (אפילו הכי). Greek: 'did not dare bring a railing accusation' (οὐκ ἐτόλμησεν κρίσιν ἐπενεγκεῖν βλασφημίας). Greek elaborates where Hebrew is concise.
translation_notes: 'Grave' for qever — critical to preserve the Deuteronomy 34:6 connection. The mystery of Moses' unknown burial site is the background.
'Punish' for ya'anosh — judicial severity, not mere verbal correction.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 34:5-6 — 'So Moses the servant of YHWH died there... and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab... but no man knows his burial-place (קבורתו) to this day.' The Hebrew Jude's use of qever ties directly to this Torah passage.

verses.translation: But these curse{H7043} and do not know{H3045} anything{H1697}, and even what they know{H3045} they despise{H959}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'what they know, they despise' (מבזים — 'despise'). Greek: 'what they know naturally, as unreasoning beasts, in those things they are corrupted' (ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα ἐπίστανται, ἐν τούτοις φθείρονται). Greek adds 'as unreasoning beasts' and says they are 'corrupted' (φθείρονται), not that they 'despise.' Hebrew is concise; Greek elaborates with an animal comparison.
Hebrew: 'despise' (מבזים). Greek: 'are corrupted/destroyed' (φθείρονται). Different outcome — contempt vs. self-destruction.

verses.translation: And woe{H1945} to them, for they walk{H1980} upon the way{H1870} of Qayin{H7014}, and fall{H5307} into the trial{H5254} of Bil'am{H1109} for the sake of some profits, and are killed{H2026} because of the dispute{H4066} of Qorach{H7141}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמַּחֲלֹוקֶת (ha-machaloqet — 'the dispute', from cheleq/chaloq H4066) — the specific Hebrew/rabbinic term for a legal-religious controversy or dispute. Greek has ἀντιλογία ('contradiction/gainsaying'). Machaloqet is THE standard term in Hebrew tradition for the 'dispute of Korah' (Numbers 16), where Korah challenged the priestly authority of Aaron. This term became a cornerstone of rabbinic discourse (Pirqei Avot 5:17 — 'Any machaloqet that is for the sake of Heaven will endure'). A back-translator from Greek ἀντιλογία would use a general word like הִתְנַגְּדוּת ('opposition'), not the legally loaded machaloqet.

Uses נִסָּיוֹן (nisayon — 'trial/test', from nasah H5254). Greek has πλάνη ('error/wandering'). A trial/test is something that reveals character; an error is a mistake. The Hebrew says Bil'am's situation was a TEST (cf. God testing Abraham — נִסָּה, Gen 22:1); the Greek says it was an ERROR. A back-translator from Greek would use תְּעִיָּה (te'iyah — 'wandering') or שְׁגִיאָה ('error'), not nisayon ('trial').

Uses נֶהֱרָגִים (neheragim — 'are killed', from harag H2026). Greek has ἀπώλοντο ('perished'). Hebrew harag is specifically to kill/slay — the verb used for Cain killing Abel (Gen 4:8 — וַיַּהַרְגֵהוּ). The Hebrew creates a literary bracket: they walk in Cain's WAY (who killed), and they ARE KILLED in Korah's dispute. A back-translator would use אָבְדוּ ('perished'), not the Cain-echoing harag.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the trial of Bil'am' (test of character). Greek: 'the error of Balaam' (πλάνῃ — mistake/wandering).
Hebrew: 'are killed' (harag — slain). Greek: 'perished' (ἀπώλοντο — destroyed).
Hebrew: 'the dispute of Qorach' (machaloqet — legal controversy). Greek: 'the gainsaying of Korah' (ἀντιλογίᾳ — contradiction).
translation_notes: 'Dispute' for machaloqet — preserving the Hebrew legal/religious controversy term that became central to rabbinic thought.
'Trial' for nisayon — Bil'am was tested by God (Num 22-24) and eventually failed the test by counseling Balaq to seduce Israel (Num 31:16).
'Killed' for neheragim — echoing the verb of Cain's murder, creating a literary inclusio with the verse's opening.
textual_notes: Numbers 16 — Korah's dispute (machaloqet) challenged Moses and Aaron's authority. He and his followers were swallowed by the earth (Num 16:32). The Hebrew Jude warns that those who follow this pattern of disputing legitimate authority meet the same fate — they 'are killed.'

verses.translation: And they are masters{H1167} of pride with your gifts, and they are like clouds{H6051} without{H1097} water{H4325} that go{H1980} in the wind{H7307}, and trees that bear{H5375} no fruit{H6529}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בַּעֲלֵי גֵאוּת ('masters of pride', from ba'al H1167). Greek has σπιλάδες ('hidden rocks/blemishes') and ἀφόβως ἑαυτοὺς ποιμαίνοντες ('feeding themselves without fear'). Completely different imagery — Hebrew accuses them of PRIDE, Greek calls them HIDDEN DANGERS. A back-translator from Greek would never produce 'masters of pride' from 'hidden rocks.'

Uses מַתְּנוֹתֵיכֶם (matnotekhem — 'your gifts'). Greek has ἀγάπαις ὑμῶν ('your love-feasts'). GIFTS vs. LOVE-FEASTS — entirely different settings. The Hebrew warns about proud men exploiting your charitable gifts; the Greek warns about them infiltrating your communal meals. A back-translator from Greek ἀγάπαις would use סְעוּדוֹת or מִשְׁתּוֹת ('feasts'), not matanot ('gifts').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'masters of pride with your gifts.' Greek: 'hidden rocks in your love-feasts, feeding themselves without fear.' Different metaphor, different setting.
Hebrew: 'trees that bear no fruit' (concise). Greek: 'autumn trees, fruitless, twice dead, uprooted' (φθινοπωρινά ἄκαρπα δὶς ἀποθανόντα ἐκριζωθέντα — four descriptors). Greek dramatically elaborates.
Hebrew omits 'feeding themselves without fear' (ἑαυτοὺς ποιμαίνοντες) entirely.
translation_notes: 'Masters of pride' for ba'alei ge'ut — the ba'al construction in Hebrew designates someone characterized by a quality (cf. ba'al chalom — 'master of dreams', Gen 37:19).
אִילָנוֹת (ilanot — 'trees') is a later Hebrew/Aramaic form, not the OT standard עֵץ (ets). No standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: And like waves{H1530} of the sea{H3220} that cast-out{H7993} mire{H7516} and mud{H2916}.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 57:20: כִּי הָרְשָׁעִים כַּיָּם נִגְרָשׁ... וַיִּגְרְשׁוּ מֵימָיו רֶפֶשׁ וָטִיט — 'For the wicked are like the troubled sea... and its waters cast up mire (refesh) and mud (tit).' The Hebrew uses Isaiah's exact vocabulary: רֶפֶשׁ (refesh — 'mire', H7516) and טִיט (tit — 'mud/clay', H2916). Greek has ἐπαφρίζοντα τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας ('foaming out their own shame'). A back-translator from Greek would write מַקְצִיפִים בּוּשָׁתָם ('foaming their shame'), NOT the Isaiah 57:20 word-pair refesh va-tit. The Hebrew preserves the prophetic quotation; the Greek paraphrases with an entirely different image.

Greek adds an entire clause absent from Hebrew: ἀστέρες πλανῆται οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετήρηται ('wandering stars for whom the blackness of darkness is reserved forever'). The Hebrew verse 13 contains only the sea/wave image; the Greek adds a separate cosmic image. This suggests the Hebrew is the more original, concise form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'cast out mire and mud' (Isaiah 57:20 quotation). Greek: 'foaming out their own shame' (ἐπαφρίζοντα τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας). Different content entirely.
Greek adds 'wandering stars for whom is reserved the blackness of darkness forever' — an entire clause absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Mire and mud' for refesh va-tit — preserving the Isaiah 57:20 word-pair. These are physical, concrete terms for sediment cast up by turbulent water.
textual_notes: Isaiah 57:20 — 'But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire (רֶפֶשׁ) and mud (טִיט).' The Hebrew Jude applies this prophetic image directly to the false teachers. The connection is unmistakable in Hebrew but completely absent from the Greek.

verses.translation: And also of these prophesied{H5012} Chanokh{H2585}, the seventh{H7637} from Adam{H121}, and said{H559}: See{H7200}! The Lord{H113} will come{H935} with thousands{H505} of thousands{H505}, myriads{H7233} of holy-ones{H6918}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲנוֹךְ (Chanokh, H2585) — the Hebrew name as it appears in Genesis 5:18-24. This explicitly names Enoch as a prophet and quotes his prophecy, supporting the quotation of the Book of Enoch (1 Enoch 1:9). The Hebrew text makes the Enoch-attribution unmistakable.

Uses future tense יָבֹא (yavo — 'will come'). Greek has aorist ἦλθεν ('came' — past tense). The Hebrew treats the coming as a future prophetic event; the Greek presents it as a completed (prophetic past) event. A back-translator from Greek aorist would use בָּא (ba — 'came'), not the imperfect/future yavo.

Uses אַלְפֵי אֲלָפִים רִבְבוֹת ('thousands of thousands, myriads') — a compound Hebrew number expression echoing Daniel 7:10: אֶלֶף אַלְפִים... וְרִבּוֹ רִבְבָן ('a thousand thousands... and myriad myriads'). Greek has ἁγίαις μυριάσιν αὐτοῦ ('his holy myriads/ten-thousands') — a simpler expression. The Hebrew preserves the Danielic number formula; the Greek simplifies. A back-translator from Greek would write רְבָבוֹת קְדוֹשָׁיו ('his holy myriads'), not the double expression 'thousands of thousands, myriads.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'will come' (future). Greek: 'came' (aorist/past). Different tense.
Hebrew: 'thousands of thousands, myriads of holy ones' (elaborate Danielic formula). Greek: 'his holy myriads' (simpler).
Hebrew: 'the Lord' (האדון). Greek: 'the Lord' (Κύριος). This matches.
translation_notes: The explicit naming of Chanokh 'the seventh from Adam' as a prophet strongly supports the historicity of the Enoch tradition. The 'seventh from Adam' genealogy matches Genesis 5:3-18 exactly (Adam → Seth → Enosh → Kenan → Mahalalel → Yared → Chanokh).
textual_notes: 1 Enoch 1:9 — 'Behold, he comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment upon them.' The Hebrew Jude's version is closer to Daniel 7:10's number formula than to the extant Ethiopic 1 Enoch text, suggesting access to a Hebrew/Aramaic Enoch tradition.

verses.translation: To execute{H6213} judgment{H4941} upon the wicked{H7563} for the sake of their evil{H7451} deeds{H4639}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew is extremely concise — a single clause. Greek has a fourfold repetition of ἀσεβ- ('ungodly'): ἐξελέγξαι πάντας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς... ἔργων ἀσεβείας... ὧν ἠσέβησαν... ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς. The Hebrew uses רְשָׁעִים (resha'im — 'the wicked') once. A back-translator from the rhetorically elaborate Greek would reproduce some of the repetition, not condense it to six words.
Uses מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, H4941) — THE foundational Hebrew word for justice/judgment, used hundreds of times in Torah. The Hebrew continues the Torah-legal framework of the entire epistle.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: one clause (six words). Greek: an elaborate sentence with fourfold 'ungodly' repetition plus 'hard things they have spoken against him' (σκληρῶν ὧν ἐλάλησαν κατ' αὐτοῦ). The 'hard words' clause is entirely absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: רשעים ('wicked' — moral category). Greek: ἀσεβεῖς ('ungodly/impious' — religious category). Different nuance.
translation_notes: 'Judgment' for mishpat — the standard OT legal term encompassing justice, verdict, and legal procedure.

verses.translation: For there is nothing{H369} reliable{H3559} in his mouth{H6310}; their inward-part{H7130} is destruction{H1942}; their throat{H1627} is an open{H6605} grave{H6913}; their tongue{H3956} they make smooth{H2505}.

one_way_hebrew: THIS IS THE STRONGEST ONE-WAY MARKER IN THE ENTIRE EPISTLE. The Hebrew is a VERBATIM quote from Psalm 5:10 (Hebrew numbering; 5:9 English): כִּי אֵין בְּפִיהוּ נְכוֹנָה קִרְבָּם הַוּוֹת קֶבֶר פָּתוּחַ גְּרוֹנָם לְשׁוֹנָם יַחֲלִיקוּן. Word for word, letter for letter, the Hebrew Jude quotes David's psalm about the wicked. The Greek of Jude 16 says something COMPLETELY DIFFERENT: Οὗτοί εἰσιν γογγυσταί μεμψίμοιροι κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι καὶ τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν λαλεῖ ὑπέρογκα θαυμάζοντες πρόσωπα ὠφελείας χάριν — 'These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaks great swelling words, showing favoritism for advantage.' There is NO open grave, NO smooth tongue, NO destruction in their inward part. The Greek and Hebrew say COMPLETELY DIFFERENT THINGS at this verse. No back-translator from the Greek could EVER produce Psalm 5:10. This is irrefutable evidence of Hebrew textual independence.

Note that Romans 3:13 ALSO quotes this same Psalm 5:10 (via the LXX) in Paul's catena of OT passages about human wickedness: τάφος ἀνεῳγμένος ὁ λάρυγξ αὐτῶν ταῖς γλώσσαις αὐτῶν ἐδολιοῦσαν ('their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they have practiced deceit'). Paul considered this Psalm authoritative for describing the wicked. The Hebrew Jude author applies the same Psalm to false teachers — a natural move for a Hebrew author steeped in the Psalms.
greek_deviations: TOTAL DIVERGENCE. Hebrew: Psalm 5:10 verbatim — 'For there is nothing reliable in his mouth; their inward part is destruction; their throat is an open grave; their tongue they make smooth.' Greek: 'These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaks great swelling words, showing favoritism for advantage.' The only shared element is the word 'mouth' (פה/στόμα), but even its usage differs entirely.
contradictions: This verse presents the most radical divergence between the Hebrew and Greek texts in the entire epistle. They are not variant translations of the same source — they are two entirely different texts. The Hebrew is a Psalm quotation; the Greek is original prose. This can only be explained if the Hebrew is the source text and the Greek translator freely paraphrased, or if these represent two genuinely independent textual traditions.
translation_notes: 'Reliable' for nekhonah (from kun H3559 — 'to be firm/established') — nothing in their speech is stable or trustworthy.
'Destruction' for havvot (H1942) — the same word as in Psalm 5:10 and related to the 'howling waste' imagery.
'Make smooth' for yachiliqun (from chalaq H2505 — 'to be smooth/slippery') — flattery, deceptive speech that slides past defenses.
textual_notes: Psalm 5:10 (Hebrew) — כִּי אֵין בְּפִיהוּ נְכוֹנָה קִרְבָּם הַוּוֹת קֶבֶר־פָּתוּחַ גְּרוֹנָם לְשׁוֹנָם יַחֲלִיקוּן. The Hebrew Jude reproduces this verbatim — no adaptation, no paraphrase, no modification. This is a direct Scripture quotation embedded in the text.

The Psalm context is David's prayer against the wicked who speak falsehood: 'For there is no faithfulness in their mouth; their inward part is destruction; their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue' (Ps 5:9-10). The Hebrew Jude applies this to the false teachers described throughout the epistle.

verses.translation: But you, beloved{H157} brothers{H251}, remember{H2142} the word{H1697} that was spoken{H559} from the beginning by the sent-ones{H7971} of our Lord{H113} Yeshua{H3442} the Mashiach{H4899}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שְׁלוּחִים (sheluchim — 'sent-ones', from shalach H7971) — the same native Hebrew term used in verse 1 (שליח) and in Revelation 21:14 (שלוחים). Greek has ἀποστόλων ('apostles'). Consistent Hebrew vocabulary across the corpus. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as אפוסטולים or use some other equivalent, not independently and consistently produce the Hebrew sheluchim.

Uses הַדִיבּוּר (ha-dibbur — 'the word/speech') — singular, with the definite article. Greek has τῶν ῥημάτων ('the words' — plural). The Hebrew treats the apostolic message as a single, unified 'word'; the Greek treats it as multiple 'sayings.' Different conceptualization.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: שלוחים ('sent-ones'). Greek: ἀποστόλων ('apostles'). Native Hebrew vs. Greek title.
Hebrew: 'the word' (singular — הדיבור). Greek: 'the words' (plural — τῶν ῥημάτων).
Hebrew: 'from the beginning' (מכתחילה). Greek: 'which were spoken before' (τῶν προειρημένων). Different temporal framing.
translation_notes: 'Sent-ones' for sheluchim — maintaining consistency with verse 1 and the broader Hebrew Gospels corpus.

verses.translation: That they said{H559} to you: In the latter{H319} days{H3117} there shall be among you scoffers{H3887} who walk{H1980} after{H310} their lusts{H8378}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים (acharit hayamim — 'the latter days', H319 + H3117) — THE standard Hebrew prophetic formula for the end times, appearing in Genesis 49:1, Numbers 24:14, Deuteronomy 4:30, 31:29, Isaiah 2:2, Jeremiah 23:20, 30:24, 48:47, 49:39, Ezekiel 38:16, Daniel 2:28, 10:14, Hosea 3:5, Micah 4:1. Greek has ἐν ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ ('in the last time'). A back-translator from Greek would write בָּעֵת הָאַחֲרוֹנָה ('in the last time'), not the specific prophetic formula acharit hayamim. The Hebrew author naturally reaches for the Torah/Prophets formula; no translator would independently reconstruct it from the Greek.

Uses לֵצָנִים (letsanim — 'scoffers', from luts H3887) — the specific Wisdom Literature term for arrogant mockers who refuse correction (Proverbs 1:22, 9:7-8, 13:1, 14:6, 15:12, 19:29, 21:24, 29:8; Psalm 1:1). Greek has ἐμπαῖκται ('mockers'). While semantically similar, the Hebrew letz is a technical wisdom term with a rich OT profile. A back-translator from Greek would use מְלַעֲגִים (mela'agim — 'mockers') or a general term, not the wisdom-specific letsanim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in the latter days' (אחרית הימים — prophetic formula). Greek: 'in the last time' (ἐν ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ). Different expression.
Hebrew: לצנים (scoffers — Wisdom Literature term). Greek: ἐμπαῖκται (mockers — general).
Greek adds τῶν ἀσεβειῶν ('of ungodliness') after 'their lusts' — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Latter days' for acharit hayamim — the prophetic formula, not merely 'last time.'
'Scoffers' for letsanim — preserving the Proverbs/Psalms wisdom vocabulary. The letz is not merely someone who mocks, but one who arrogantly rejects all correction (Prov 9:7-8).
textual_notes: Psalm 1:1 — 'Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked... nor sits in the seat of the scoffers (לֵצִים).' The Hebrew Jude's use of letsanim places these false teachers in the same category as Psalm 1's scoffers — the ultimate negative archetype of Wisdom Literature.

verses.translation: And these are in the flesh{H1320} and not in the spirit{H7307}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses the basar/ruach (flesh/spirit) dichotomy — בָּשָׂר (basar, H1320) vs. רוּחַ (ruach, H7307). This is the standard OT contrast (Gen 6:3 — 'My spirit shall not strive with man forever, for he is flesh'; Isa 31:3 — 'The Egyptians are men and not God; their horses are flesh and not spirit'). Greek has ψυχικοί πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες ('soulish/natural, not having spirit'). The Greek introduces the three-tier anthropology of pneuma/psyche/soma; the Hebrew maintains the simpler basar/ruach binary of the OT. A back-translator from Greek ψυχικοί would use נַפְשִׁיִּים ('soulish'), not basar ('flesh').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in the flesh and not in the spirit' (basar/ruach binary). Greek: 'soulish, not having spirit' (ψυχικοί πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες). Different anthropological framework.
Greek adds ἀποδιορίζοντες ('those who cause divisions/separate') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: The basar/ruach contrast preserves the OT framework. This is not Platonic dualism (body vs. soul) but the Hebrew concept of human weakness (basar) vs. divine power (ruach).
textual_notes: Genesis 6:3 and Isaiah 31:3 establish the basar/ruach contrast as foundational to Hebrew theology — humanity in its weakness vs. divine enabling power.

verses.translation: But you, beloved{H157} brothers{H251}, strengthen{H2388} yourselves in your faith{H530} by the hand{H3027} of the Holy{H6944} Spirit{H7307}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עַל יַד (al yad — 'by the hand of', H3027) — a standard Hebrew idiom meaning 'through the agency of' (Num 15:23, 2 Sam 12:25, 1 Kings 16:7, Jer 37:2, Hag 1:1). Greek has ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ ('in the Holy Spirit'). 'By the hand of' implies the Spirit as agent; 'in the Spirit' implies location/sphere. A back-translator from the simple Greek preposition ἐν would write בְּ ('in'), not the idiomatic al yad.

Uses חַזְּקוּ (chazqu — 'strengthen', piel of chazaq H2388) — the same verb used in verse 3 (תחזקו). Greek has ἐποικοδομοῦντες ('building up'). The Hebrew calls for strengthening (military/fortification metaphor); the Greek calls for building (construction metaphor). These are different images. A back-translator from Greek would use בּוֹנִים (bonim — 'building'), not chazaq.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'strengthen yourselves' (fortification). Greek: 'building up yourselves' (construction). Different metaphor.
Hebrew: 'by the hand of the Holy Spirit' (agency). Greek: 'in the Holy Spirit' (sphere/location).
Greek adds προσευχόμενοι ('praying') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'By the hand of' for al yad — the Hebrew agency idiom. The Holy Spirit is the agent of strengthening.

verses.translation: And stand{H5975} in the love{H160} of YHWH{H3068}, and watch{H6822} for the compassion{H7356} from our Lord{H113} Yeshua{H3442}, unto life{H2416} forever{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְצַפִּים (tetsapim — 'watch/look out for', from tsafah H6822) — the prophetic WATCHTOWER verb, used for a lookout stationed on a height (2 Sam 13:34, 2 Kings 9:17, Isa 21:6, Hab 2:1, Mic 7:7). Greek has προσδεχόμενοι ('awaiting/receiving'). The Hebrew pictures a watchman on a tower scanning the horizon for the coming compassion; the Greek simply waits. A back-translator from Greek would use מְחַכִּים (mechakkim — 'waiting') or מְצַפִּים in a more generic sense, but the watchtower imagery is distinctly Hebrew prophetic vocabulary.

Uses רַחֲמִים (rachamim — 'compassion', H7356) — from the root רחם (rechem — 'womb'). This is the visceral, womb-deep mercy unique to Hebrew. Greek has ἔλεος ('mercy'). Rachamim is deeper than mercy — it is the gut-wrenching compassion a mother feels for her child (1 Kings 3:26, Isa 49:15). A back-translator from Greek ἔλεος would use חֶסֶד or חֶנָּה, not the womb-rooted rachamim.

Uses תַעַמְדוּ (ta'amdu — 'stand', from amad H5975). Greek has τηρήσατε ('keep/guard'). Standing and keeping are different — one implies a military stance (holding position), the other implies preservation. A back-translator from Greek would use שִׁמְרוּ (shimru — 'keep'), not amad.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'stand in the love of YHWH' (military stance). Greek: 'keep yourselves in the love of God' (preservation).
Hebrew: 'watch for the compassion' (prophetic watchtower verb). Greek: 'looking for the mercy' (general expectation).
Hebrew: rachamim ('compassion' — womb-rooted). Greek: ἔλεος ('mercy' — general).
translation_notes: 'Watch' for tetsapim — the prophetic lookout verb. Like Habakkuk 2:1: 'I will stand upon my watch, and station myself upon the tower, and watch (אֲצַפֶּה) to see what he will say to me.'
'Compassion' for rachamim — preserving the womb/visceral quality of Hebrew mercy.

verses.translation: And also you, be compassionate{H7355}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew is extremely concise — four words: 'And also you, be compassionate.' Greek is more complex: καὶ οὓς μὲν ἐλεεῖτε διακρινόμενοι ('And on some have compassion, making a distinction'). The Greek adds 'making a distinction' (διακρινόμενοι), structuring the mercy with discernment. Hebrew simply commands: BE compassionate.
translation_notes: The extreme brevity of the Hebrew command — just 'be compassionate' — is characteristic of Hebrew imperative style. Contrast the Greek's qualified, nuanced instruction.

verses.translation: But [...] some of you with good{H2896} deeds{H4639}, and distance-yourselves{H7368} from the sinners{H2400}.

one_way_hebrew: Contains a visible lacuna — brackets [  ] indicating a gap in the Hebrew manuscript. This is a mark of textual honesty: the Hebrew copyist preserved the gap rather than filling it. Greek has a complete text: οὓς δὲ ἐν φόβῳ σῴζετε ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες ('and others save with fear, snatching them out of the fire'). If the Hebrew were a back-translation from the complete Greek, there would be no reason to introduce a lacuna. The gap proves this is a genuine manuscript tradition, not a translation.

Uses תִּרְחֲקוּ (tirchaku — 'distance yourselves', from rachaq H7368) — a spatial separation verb. Greek has μισοῦντες... τὸν χιτῶνα ('hating even the garment defiled by the flesh'). Hebrew: physically distance from sinners. Greek: hate the contaminated clothing. Completely different metaphors. A back-translator from Greek would produce an image about hating garments, not spatial distancing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew has a lacuna [  ] — Greek has no gap.
Hebrew: 'good deeds.' Greek: 'snatching from fire' (ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες). Different imagery.
Hebrew: 'distance yourselves from the sinners.' Greek: 'hating even the garment defiled by the flesh' (μισοῦντες καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐσπιλωμένον χιτῶνα). Different metaphor.
Greek adds 'with fear' (ἐν φόβῳ) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: The lacuna [  ] is preserved in translation with brackets and ellipsis to indicate the manuscript gap.
'Distance yourselves' for tirchaku — the spatial concept of maintaining separation from those who practice sin.
textual_notes: The lacuna suggests damage to the Hebrew manuscript at this point. The Zechariah 3:2 parallel to 'snatching from fire' in the Greek tradition (אוּד מֻצָּל מֵאֵשׁ — 'a brand plucked from the burning') may represent what originally filled the gap.

verses.translation: But to the one who is able{H3201} to keep{H8104} you without doubt, and to stand{H5975} you before{H6440} the Lord{H113} without any sin{H2399}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לִשְׁמֹר (lishmor — 'to keep/guard', from shamar H8104) — the Torah's central commandment verb: שָׁמַר ('observe/keep the commandments' — Deut 5:12, 6:17). Greek has φυλάξαι ('to guard'). While similar, shamar carries the full weight of Torah observance. The pairing of shamar (keep) with amad (stand before the Lord) echoes the priestly language of standing before YHWH to minister (Deut 10:8, 18:7).

Uses בְּלִי סָפֵק ('without doubt'). Greek has ἀπταίστους ('without stumbling'). Doubt vs. stumbling — inner state vs. physical action. A back-translator from Greek would write בְּלִי מִכְשׁוֹל ('without stumbling'), not the abstract 'without doubt.'

Uses לִפְנֵי הָאָדוֹן ('before the Lord', H6440). Greek has κατενώπιον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ ('before his glory'). Before THE LORD vs. before HIS GLORY — direct personal audience vs. radiant presence. A back-translator would write לִפְנֵי כְבוֹדוֹ ('before his glory'), not lifnei ha-adon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'without doubt' (inner certainty). Greek: 'without stumbling' (ἀπταίστους — physical metaphor).
Hebrew: 'before the Lord.' Greek: 'before his glory.' Different referent.
Hebrew: 'without any sin' (בלי שום חטא). Greek: 'blameless with exceeding joy' (ἀμώμους ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει). Greek adds 'with exceeding joy' — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Keep' for lishmor — the Torah-observance verb, implying divine protection that enables faithfulness.

verses.translation: To this one shall be glory{H3519} and splendor{H8597} and kingdom{H4438}, from everlasting{H5769} to everlasting{H5769}. Amen{H543}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting to everlasting') — THE standard Hebrew doxology formula from the Psalms: 1 Chronicles 16:36, Psalm 41:14, 90:2, 103:17, 106:48. Greek has καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς πάντας τοὺς αἰῶνας ('both now and to all ages'). A back-translator from Greek would write עַתָּה וּלְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים ('now and to ages of ages'), NOT the Psalter's exact formula me-olam ve-ad olam. The Hebrew doxology closes the epistle with the same words that close Books I-IV of the Psalter.

Uses כָּבוֹד וְתִפְאֶרֶת וּמַלְכוּת ('glory and splendor and kingdom') — three attributes. Greek has δόξα καὶ μεγαλωσύνη κράτος καὶ ἐξουσία ('glory and majesty, dominion and authority') — four attributes. Greek adds μεγαλωσύνη ('majesty') and replaces מלכות ('kingdom') with κράτος καὶ ἐξουσία ('dominion and authority'). The Hebrew triad kavod-tiferet-malchut echoes the 1 Chronicles 29:11 doxology: לְךָ יְהוָה הַגְּדֻלָּה וְהַגְּבוּרָה וְהַתִּפְאֶרֶת — 'Yours, O YHWH, is the greatness and the power and the splendor.'

Greek adds μόνῳ σοφῷ θεῷ σωτῆρι ἡμῶν ('to the only wise God our Savior') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew doxology is addressed simply to 'this one' (לזה — referencing the one who keeps and stands them before the Lord in v24).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three attributes (glory, splendor, kingdom). Greek: four attributes (glory, majesty, dominion, authority).
Hebrew: 'from everlasting to everlasting' (Psalter doxology formula). Greek: 'both now and to all ages' (different formula).
Greek adds 'to the only wise God our Savior' — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds 'through Jesus Christ our Lord' (διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'From everlasting to everlasting' for me-olam ve-ad olam — the Psalter's eternal formula, used to close Books I-IV of the Psalms.
'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) — beauty, glory, ornamental magnificence.
'Kingdom' for malchut (H4438) — sovereign rule, not merely 'dominion.'
textual_notes: The Hebrew doxology formula me-olam ve-ad olam closes four books of the Psalter: Ps 41:14 (Book I), Ps 72:19 (Book II — similar), Ps 89:53 (Book III), Ps 106:48 (Book IV). The Hebrew Jude uses the established liturgical formula to close the epistle — a natural move for a Hebrew author. A Greek translator would have no reason to produce this specific form.
1 Chronicles 29:11-13 — David's doxology — contains kavod and tiferet together, providing the closest OT parallel to the Hebrew Jude's closing.

chapter_notes.summary: The Hebrew Epistle of Jude contains at least 12 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek text. The single most devastating marker is verse 16: a VERBATIM quotation of Psalm 5:10 (כי אין בפיהו נכונה קרבם הוות קבר פתוח גרונם לשונם יחליקון — 'For there is nothing reliable in his mouth; their inward part is destruction; their throat is an open grave; their tongue they make smooth') where the Greek says something ENTIRELY DIFFERENT about murmurers and complainers. No back-translator from the Greek could ever produce Psalm 5:10. Other major one-way markers include: (1) verse 4's מזיד (mezid — 'presumption') — the Torah's legal term for high-handed sin vs. Greek's ἀσέλγεια ('lasciviousness'); (2) verse 7's גיהנום (Gehinnom — the Valley of Hinnom) vs. Greek's generic 'eternal fire'; (3) verse 9's הקבר של משה ('the grave of Moses') vs. Greek's 'the body of Moses' — connecting to Deuteronomy 34:6's unknown burial-place; (4) verse 11's המחלוקת של קרח ('the dispute of Korah') — the Hebrew legal/rabbinic term for religious controversy; (5) verse 13's Isaiah 57:20 verbatim quotation (רפש וטיט — 'mire and mud') vs. Greek's 'foaming out their shame'; (6) verse 18's אחרית הימים ('the latter days') — the specific Torah/Prophets eschatological formula; (7) verse 25's מעולם ועד עולם ('from everlasting to everlasting') — the Psalter doxology formula. The epistle consistently uses native Hebrew vocabulary (שליח/שלוחים not 'apostle'; נסתרים not 'kept'; חסד not 'grace'; רחמים not 'mercy'; משפט not 'judgment'; לצנים not 'mockers') and contains a textual lacuna in verse 23 that would not exist in a back-translation. Verse 14 explicitly attributes prophecy to Chanokh (Enoch), supporting the quotation of the Book of Enoch. The cumulative evidence — especially the Psalm 5:10 quotation in verse 16 — constitutes among the strongest cases for Hebrew textual priority in the entire Hebrew Gospels corpus.
